note: When Rabbi Yoḥanan was chosen to head the yeshiva over Ilfa, who was away at the time, Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast and declared that if anyone brought him a teaching from the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya that he could not show was already in the Mishna, he would fall and drown. An older man came and recited a ruling about a dying man who says, give my sons a shekel each week. Ilfa answered that the ruling follows Rabbi Meir, who says it is a mitzva to carry out the instructions of the dead, and so he met the challenge.
why: The Gemara has just been explaining a mishna, attributed to Rabbi Meir, in which a third party must carry out a dead father's instructions; Ilfa's answer rests on that same mishna and Rabbi Meir's principle. Afterward the Gemara gives the final ruling on the sons' allowance.

note: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, he called in his sons. He told them to honor their mother (the Gemara explains she was their stepmother), to keep his lamp lit, his table set and his bed made, and said Yosef Ḥeifani and Shimon Efrati, who served him in life, would serve him in death. After his death he came home every Shabbat eve, until a neighbor knocked and his maidservant said, Quiet, Rabbi is sitting; then he never came again. His two attendants died before him. He also summoned the Sages, told them not to eulogize him in the small towns and to reopen the yeshiva after thirty days, and named his son Shimon the Sage, his son Gamliel the Nasi, and Ḥanina bar Ḥama head of the yeshiva.
